Further information: [List of Brown University buildings](/wiki/List_of_Brown_University_buildings "List of Brown University buildings")

Brown's main campus, comprises 235 buildings and 143 acres (58 ha) in the [East Side](/wiki/East_Side,_Providence,_Rhode_Island "East Side, Providence, Rhode Island") neighborhood of College Hill. The university's central campus sits on a 15-acre (6.1 ha) block bounded by Waterman, Prospect, George, and [Thayer Streets](/wiki/Thayer_Street "Thayer Street"); newer buildings extend northward, eastward, and southward. Brown's core, historic campus, constructed primarily between 1770 and 1926, is defined by three greens: the Front or Quiet Green, the Main or College Green, and the Ruth J. Simmons Quadrangle (historically known as Lincoln Field).[[63]](#cite_note-campus_heritage2-68)[[64]](#cite_note-69) A brick and wrought-iron fence punctuated by decorative gates and arches traces the block's perimeter. This section of campus is primarily [Georgian](/wiki/Georgian_architecture "Georgian architecture") and [Richardsonian Romanesque](/wiki/Richardsonian_Romanesque "Richardsonian Romanesque") in its architectural character.[[63]](#cite_note-campus_heritage2-68)

To the south of the central campus are academic buildings and residential quadrangles, including Wriston, Keeney, and Gregorian quadrangles. Immediately to the east of the campus core sit Sciences Park and Brown's [School of Engineering](/wiki/Brown_University_School_of_Engineering "Brown University School of Engineering"). North of the central campus are performing and visual arts facilities, life sciences labs, and the Pembroke Campus, which houses both dormitories and academic buildings. Facing the western edge of the central campus sit two of the Brown's seven libraries, the [John Hay Library](/wiki/John_Hay_Library "John Hay Library") and the [John D. Rockefeller Jr. Library](/wiki/John_D._Rockefeller_Jr._Library "John D. Rockefeller Jr. Library").

Beginning in 1980, [Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory](/wiki/LIGO "LIGO") (LIGO) was designed and constructed by a team of scientists from [California Institute of Technology](/wiki/California_Institute_of_Technology "California Institute of Technology"), MIT, and industrial contractors, and funded by the [National Science Foundation](/wiki/National_Science_Foundation "National Science Foundation"). It was designed to open the field of [gravitational-wave astronomy](/wiki/Gravitational-wave_astronomy "Gravitational-wave astronomy") through the detection of [gravitational waves](/wiki/Gravitational_wave "Gravitational wave") predicted by [general relativity](/wiki/General_relativity "General relativity").[[316]](#cite_note-333) Gravitational waves were [detected for the first time](/wiki/First_observation_of_gravitational_waves "First observation of gravitational waves") by the LIGO detector in 2015. For contributions to the LIGO detector and the observation of gravitational waves, two Caltech physicists, [Kip Thorne](/wiki/Kip_Thorne "Kip Thorne") and [Barry Barish](/wiki/Barry_Barish "Barry Barish"), and MIT physicist [Rainer Weiss](/wiki/Rainer_Weiss "Rainer Weiss") won the [Nobel Prize in physics](/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_physics "Nobel Prize in physics") in 2017.[[317]](#cite_note-334) Weiss, who is also an MIT graduate, designed the laser interferometric technique, which served as the essential blueprint for the LIGO.[[318]](#cite_note-335)

The decision to send William to Eton broke with royal tradition, as his father and grandfather had both attended [Gordonstoun](/wiki/Gordonstoun "Gordonstoun").[[37]](#cite_note-40) The royal family and the press agreed that William would be allowed to study free from media intrusion in exchange for periodic official updates.[[38]](#cite_note-41) In June 1991, he was admitted to the [Royal Berkshire Hospital](/wiki/Royal_Berkshire_Hospital "Royal Berkshire Hospital") after being accidentally hit on the forehead by a fellow pupil wielding a golf club. fanoutqa_001992.t: Epidemiology of cancer :: Rates and mortality :: Incidence of a second cancer in survivors :: chunk_0007
fanoutqa_001992.x:
Epidemiology of cancer :: Rates and mortality :: Incidence of a second cancer in survivors :: chunk_0007
In 2003, in the developed world, one in three people developed cancer during their lifetimes. If all cancer patients survived and cancer occurred randomly, the normal lifetime odds of developing a second primary cancer (not the first cancer spreading to a new site) would be one in nine.[[31]](#cite_note-Rheingold03-31) However, [cancer survivors](/wiki/Cancer_survivor "Cancer survivor") have an increased risk of developing a second primary cancer, and the odds in 2003 were about one in 4.5.[[31]](#cite_note-Rheingold03-31) About half of these second primaries can be attributed to the normal one-in-nine risk associated with random chance.[[31]](#cite_note-Rheingold03-31)

The increased risk is believed to be primarily due to the same risk factors that produced the first cancer, such as the person's genetic profile, alcohol and tobacco use, obesity, and environmental exposures, and partly due, in some cases, to the treatment for the first cancer, which might have included mutagenic chemotherapeutic drugs or radiation.[[31]](#cite_note-Rheingold03-31) Cancer survivors may be more likely to comply with recommended screening, and may be more likely than average to detect cancers.[[31]](#cite_note-Rheingold03-31)

A [transit](/wiki/Transit_(astronomy) "Transit (astronomy)") of Venus is the appearance of Venus in front of the Sun, during [inferior conjunction](/wiki/Inferior_conjunction "Inferior conjunction"). Since the orbit of Venus is slightly inclined relative to Earth's orbit, most inferior conjunctions with Earth, which occur every [synodic period](/wiki/Synodic_period "Synodic period") of 1.6 years, do not produce a transit of Venus. Consequently, Venus transits only occur when an inferior conjunction takes place during some days of June or December, when the orbits of Venus and Earth cross a straight line with the Sun.[[186]](#cite_note-188) This results in Venus transiting above Earth in a sequence currently of 8 years, 105.5 years, 8 years and 121.5 years, forming cycles of 243 years.

Historically, transits of Venus were important, because they allowed astronomers to determine the size of the [astronomical unit](/wiki/Astronomical_unit "Astronomical unit"), and hence the size of the Solar System as shown by [Jeremiah Horrocks](/wiki/Jeremiah_Horrocks "Jeremiah Horrocks") in [1639 with the first known observation](/wiki/Transit_of_Venus,_1639 "Transit of Venus, 1639") of a Venus transit (after history's first observed planetary [transit in 1631, of Mercury](/wiki/Transit_of_Mercury "Transit of Mercury")).[[187]](#cite_note-Kollerstrom_1998-189)
